name: sekkei
summary: A design-first harness for LLM coding agents: a checkable architecture graph, a deterministic linter, self-contained work-package briefs, a plan, and drift checks against the code.
goals: A design schema rich enough for real systems and small enough for an LLM to emit correctly.
Every lint rule deterministic, identified, and covered by a planted-defect test.
Briefs that let one agent implement one package without reading the rest of the design.
A closed loop: brief, implementation, completion report, acceptance, next packages.

rules: Standard library only at runtime (the anthropic package is an optional extra used by sekkei/llm.py only).
Python 3.11+; type hints everywhere; dataclasses for the model.
No fuzzy matching: every diagnostic must be reproducible from the design alone.
Import direction: cli -> {brief, drift, state, render, llm, rules, graph} -> model; never upward.
definition_of_done: No file outside the package's write scope was changed.

requirements.statement: The design file describes requirements, components, interfaces with operations, entities, flows, decisions, risks, work packages and acceptance checks, and round-trips through JSON without loss.
Every lint rule is deterministic, has a stable id, a fixed severity and a fix hint, and is covered by a planted-defect test that the meta-test enforces.

A brief for a work package contains its goal, the requirements it satisfies verbatim, the contracts it implements, the contracts it consumes, its write scope, the conventions, its acceptance checks and the completion-report template, and nothing about other packages.
The plan orders work packages into waves such that every package's dependencies lie in earlier waves, and reports the size-weighted critical path.
For Python code the drift check reports missing component paths, missing operations, parameter mismatches and undeclared imports between components.
A completion report is accepted only if every acceptance check of the package passed and every touched file is inside the package's write scope; acceptance unlocks dependents.
No runtime dependency outside the Python standard library; Python 3.11 or newer.
Linting and drift-checking this repository's own design finishes fast enough to run on every commit.

metric.name: wall time of `sekkei lint` plus `sekkei check` on examples/self on a laptop

requirements.statement: A human can author a design in a small Python DSL that yields the same model as the JSON.

sekkei designs from a requirements text: it drafts a design with a model, feeds lint diagnostics back until clean, has the model review the design against a senior-architect checklist, revises, and lints again; the model runs through the local Claude Code CLI (no API key) or the anthropic SDK.
A command line exposes every operation with a default design file, JSON output where an orchestrator would consume it, and exit code 1 on errors.

Two versions of a design can be compared, listing added, removed and changed elements and the work packages whose briefs became stale; a completion report against a stale brief is rejected unless forced.

sekkei designs a system from a requirements text without any model: it segments the text into requirement units with their numbers, recognises capability patterns and quality attributes from a catalogue, synthesises components, interfaces with operations, entities, flows, decisions, risks and work packages, scores every decision against the active qualities and constraints, repairs and lints the result, and reviews its own gaps.
The design engine is deterministic: the same requirements text yields byte-identical output.

metric.name: designs from two runs on the same text that differ

requirements.statement: Every element of a generated design traces to the input sentences and the catalogue rules that produced it, and the engine states which requirements it did not recognise instead of hiding them.

Besides the design, the engine hands over an architect's notes: the questions the text leaves open with the assumption taken meanwhile, capacity estimates with formulas and inputs, an effort and schedule estimate, a STRIDE-lite threat model whose threats become risks in the design, and a requirements template.

The engine answers its own open questions from evidence in the text or defensible defaults, appends the answers to the requirements so they shape the design, and records each as a proposed decision with the options considered and what to change if the real answer differs.

Every functional requirement no pattern recognised gets an owner: an existing specific component by word overlap, the surface and core for a human use case, or a newly synthesised component named from the sentence's verb class and object, wired into the design and packaged.

A human can design in dialogue: free sentences become classified requirement bullets, the engine re-designs after every turn and asks one thing at a time in architect order (placements to confirm, stack, load and quality, data/security/operations/cost, close decisions), each with its proposal; answers are normalised into canonical bullets so the requirements file reproduces the design without the dialogue; the session resumes from saved state.

Requirements may be written in Japanese: a glossary, a number grammar and a particle-driven reorder rewrite each sentence into the engine's canonical English; every rewrite is reported next to its source and words the glossary does not know are listed, never guessed.
The whole hand-over package is derived from the design: executive summary, ADRs, C4 diagrams, risk register, FMEA, roadmap, RACI, SLOs, a cost model whose unit prices are never guessed, and runbooks.

The design is attacked with the requirements as the oracle: inert sentences, lost numbers, contradictions, fragile decisions, assumption load, non-determinism and deliverable drift are reported with a severity.

Specifications as engineers write them are read: numbered headings without '#', requirement tables, user stories in headings, Given/When/Then, checkboxes, nested bullets, speaker labels, TODO and out-of-scope lines, DECIDED lines, front matter and 'alternatives considered'; every fold is reported in the notes.
Work packages export as tracker issues (Markdown bodies, a GitHub CLI script in dependency order, CSV) and the HTTP interfaces export as an OpenAPI 3.0 skeleton.

components.name: Brief
components.responsibility: Self-contained work-package briefs, their fingerprint, and the report template.

components.name: Drift
components.responsibility: Design-versus-code checks over Python sources using ast.

components.name: State
components.responsibility: Progress state in .sekkei/state.json, brief fingerprints, and completion-report acceptance.

components.name: DSL
components.responsibility: Python builder for authoring designs by hand.

components.name: Design engine
components.responsibility: Model backends (Claude Code CLI, anthropic SDK, fake), the architect and review prompts, and the draft/review/revise pipeline.

components.name: CLI
components.responsibility: argparse front end over every module.

components.name: Starter
components.responsibility: The example design written by `sekkei init`.

components.name: Diff
components.responsibility: Element-level comparison of two design versions and the packages they affect.

components.name: Text analysis
components.responsibility: Sentence segmentation, sections, modality, the quantity grammar, actors, verbs and nouns.

components.name: Catalogue
components.responsibility: The knowledge base: archetypes, entity and flow templates, decision points with scored options, risks, capability patterns with signals, quality tactics, constraint tokens and language layouts.

components.name: Requirements analysis
components.responsibility: Turns sentences into requirement units (kind, priority, metric), matches patterns and qualities, extracts constraints, and lists what was not recognised.

components.name: Synthesis
components.responsibility: Instantiates and merges archetypes into components and interfaces, derives operations from verbs and objects, maps requirements to components, builds entities, flows, decisions, risks, conventions and work packages; records the trace.

components.name: Evaluation
components.responsibility: Scores decision options against the active qualities and constraints (utility with availability rules and stated-technology bonus) and writes the engine's review of its own gaps.

components.name: Repair
components.responsibility: Runs the linter over the synthesised design and applies the few repairs synthesis may make.

components.name: Engine facade
components.responsibility: design(text, assume): analyse, answer open questions and re-analyse, synthesise, record assumed decisions, inject threats, repair, review, notes; ask(text): questions only.

components.name: Answers
components.responsibility: Answer rules for every gap question: evidence from the text first, defensible defaults second; appends the answers to the requirements.

components.name: Interview
components.responsibility: The dialogue: prompts in architect order with proposals, canonical bullets from answers, owner and decision overrides, undo, saved state, and the read-eval loop.

components.name: Owners
components.responsibility: Owner placement for requirements no pattern recognised: word overlap with specific components, surface+core for human use cases, or a synthesised component.

components.name: Gap questions
components.responsibility: The questions an architect asks before committing, derived from what the text does not say, each with the assumption used meanwhile.

components.name: Sizing
components.responsibility: Capacity estimates (Little's law, storage, backlog) and effort/schedule from package sizes and team size, with every assumption stated.

components.name: Threat model
components.responsibility: STRIDE-lite threats per archetype, injected into the design as risks with mitigations and proofs.

components.name: Architect's notes
components.responsibility: Assembles questions, capacity, effort, threats, the self-review and the reading of the text into one Markdown report; holds the requirements template.

components.name: Japanese input
components.responsibility: Glossary, number/unit grammar, modality lexicon and particle-driven reorder that rewrite Japanese requirements into canonical English, with an audit table of every rewrite.

components.name: Structure pass
components.responsibility: Reads real-world document structure (tables, numbered headings, stories, labels, front matter) into the canonical Markdown shape the engine reads, reporting every fold.

components.name: Exports
components.responsibility: Tracker issues (bodies, gh script, CSV) and an OpenAPI 3.0 skeleton derived from the design.

components.name: Domain model
components.responsibility: Entities with typed fields, relations, state machines and invariants read from the sentences (parenthesised attribute lists, 'with A, B and C', possessives, transactional and state verbs, arrow lists); aggregates by relation.

components.name: Deliverables
components.responsibility: Executive summary, ADRs, C4, risk register, FMEA, roadmap, RACI, SLOs, cost model and runbooks derived from the design and the notes.

components.name: Red team
components.responsibility: Adversarial self-audit: re-runs the engine on perturbed requirements and compares design shapes; contradictions, lost numbers, assumption load, determinism.

decisions.title: Single source of truth for interface ownership
decisions.context: A component could list what it provides, or an interface could name its owner.

options.name: component.provides and interface.owner
cons: two lists that must agree will not

decisions.rationale: Redundant bookkeeping is where LLM-written designs go wrong first.

decisions.title: JSON as the design format
decisions.context: The file is written mostly by models and read mostly by tools.
decisions.rationale: Render exists for humans; the DSL exists for hand-authoring.

decisions.title: Work packages carry a write scope
decisions.context: Parallel agents must not edit the same files.
decisions.rationale: It is the only way to make parallel waves safe.

decisions.title: Python-only symbol and import checks
decisions.context: Drift checking needs a parser per language.

options.name: stdlib ast, Python only
cons: other languages get presence checks only

decisions.rationale: Honest partial coverage beats a dependency the user cannot install.

decisions.title: A deterministic engine rather than a model as the design engine
decisions.context: The engine must produce complete designs; a model would be more fluent but not reproducible or explainable.

options.name: rule-based engine over a catalogue
pros: every element traced to sentences and rules
says what it did not recognise
cons: finite catalogue; novel domains get a generic decomposition

options.name: model drafting checked by the linter

decisions.rationale: The harness exists to hold a line a model cannot hold for itself; the engine keeps that property. Model drafting stays as an optional extra.
decisions.consequences: Domains outside the catalogue are handled by the layered fallback and flagged in the review; growing the catalogue is the improvement path.

decisions.title: No orchestration

options.name: built-in runner
cons: ties sekkei to one agent API

decisions.rationale: The plan and the state file are the contract.

risks.description: Wording rules (group Q) produce false positives on legitimate text.
risks.mitigation: They are warnings with a fixed vocabulary and can be disabled with --disable Q.

risks.description: Dynamic or aliased imports escape the drift check, hiding an undeclared dependency.
risks.mitigation: Documented limitation; the check is ast-based and reports only what it can prove.

risks.description: A model emits keys or values outside the schema.
risks.mitigation: Tolerant loader records unknown keys (S006) and invalid values (S005) instead of failing to load.

risks.description: The catalogue does not cover a domain, so the engine produces a generic decomposition that looks complete.
risks.mitigation: Unrecognised requirements and generic components are listed in the review and as a risk in the design; the fixtures include a novel domain to keep this honest.

risks.description: The verb/object heuristics derive a wrong operation name from an unusual sentence.
risks.mitigation: Operations carry the sentence they came from in their description; the fixtures assert the expected operations.
